chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
title: Lining up speakers and the secretary's objection
summary: Fields talks to speakers before the session; his own secretary worries the resolution will invite other groups' demands.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So that was in there, and so I said I'm glad you join that attention and he said the only thing about it, it never had come up and he said today is the last day, this was early in the morning, he said we've got to see--we were just waiting around before the meeting was over--during the meeting those five days, I'd been figuring a few that were pretty good speakers, white and black, I was noticing, so I got around to a few of them and told them, look here, we got to see that this comes up, and the funny thing, everyone that I spoke to, they said, do you know that they've been evading this for about three years and I say yeah, that's what I understand.

All this was before the meeting was open, so when it opened we got to our seats and my secretary came in and the president and of course I was in there, I was delegate, as vice president. So I turned to my secretary and said this has to come and he looked up and said, oh yeah, but Fields if we bring this up,

Ernie, and pass a law like this, what is the Indian going to say, the Mexican going to say or the Jew going to say; they're going to say you've got to see that they count as well as that. I didn't say anything, but we always got along fine, but I said then, what does my secretary think, I'm ignorant? What is the connection with that? The deal definitely said that we had to merge and so I didn't say anything--
In the first place, there were no Indians or Mexican locals; there had been black locals and a white local.
